draft.title: Hypothetical Prompt Regression Testing Framework for Local LLMs
draft.body:
I'm outlining a hypothetical framework for regression testing prompts with local LLMs. The goal is to establish a repeatable process to evaluate prompt effectiveness over time, especially when making changes. This is purely a conceptual exercise at this stage. 

The proposed method involves a fixed set of 12 test prompts (F1). These prompts are designed to cover various scenarios, including those with clear answerable questions and those where information is insufficient for a definitive response (F3). 

The core of the test would be to run both the 'old' and 'new' versions of a prompt against the same local model, ensuring all other model settings remain identical (F2). The output for each prompt would be recorded. 

Currently, there are no results or measured improvements; this is strictly a design proposal (F4). The next step would be to define how to evaluate the outputs systematically. Any thoughts on structuring such a hypothetical test suite would be welcome.

The explanation of the test framework is clear and logically structured, making it understandable. It is useful as a conceptual guide for readers interested in designing prompt regression tests, though it lacks actionable evaluation metrics at this stage. The content is relevant to local LLM users and credible given the explicit caveats and no fabricated results. The title accurately reflects the content without exaggeration or sensationalism.

draft.title: Conceptualizing a Prompt Regression Test for Local LLM Development
draft.body:
This post discusses a hypothetical approach to prompt regression testing for local LLM experimentation. The intention is to create a structured method for evaluating prompt changes without any actual test runs or results yet. 

The plan is to establish a baseline using a defined set of 12 fixed test prompts (F1). This set would include prompts designed to elicit direct answers and others that are intentionally ambiguous or lack sufficient data for a conclusive answer (F3). 

To perform a hypothetical regression test, one would compare the output generated by an 'old' prompt against the output from a 'new' prompt, using the exact same model configuration and parameters for both (F2). This controlled comparison is key. 

It's important to reiterate that this is a purely theoretical exercise; no performance data or improvements have been observed or measured (F4). The focus is on the design of the testing methodology itself. Discussion on potential pitfalls or refinements to this hypothetical testing structure is invited.
